posts:
Soaring rough sleeping statistics clash with sweeping political pledges, leaving independent fact-checkers rating progress as wait and see. 🌐
Evidence: 7,541 rough sleepers in 2026, £874M funding package
#UKPolitics #Homelessness #FullFact

Stated Claim: The Prime Minister pledged immediate action and hundreds of millions in funding to end long-term rough sleeping across England.
Stated Judgement: (+1.00, +1.00) — Greater Good

Actual Reality: Ambiguous metric baselines and rising numbers mean political pledges currently outpace verifiable housing delivery on the ground.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.30, -0.40) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — Fall into Destruction.
Funding commitments exist, but vague definitions and rising street counts require strict long-term verification.

Integrity: Conditionally Sound (Hypocrisy: 1.8, Uncertainty z: 2)
Context: Full Fact assessed government pledges, noting that rough sleeping snapshot surveys and data frameworks show ongoing increases despite new funds.

The Bright Side:
Substantial funding increases and monthly data frameworks demonstrate a serious institutional attempt to track and tackle street homelessness.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing WHAT (announcing funding totals) with HOW (delivering actual stable housing for vulnerable populations).

Social Physics Analysis:
Political actors employ optimistic framing to manage public perception while administrative inertia and structural housing shortages slow real relief.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
Modal Dynamics: will be -> May be via Destructive. Stated grand futures are tempered by empirical oversight into cautious conditional steps.

The Unavoidable Truth: Ending rough sleeping demands sustained housing supply, not just short-term funding announcements.

The Unavoidable Lie: Political pledges alone instantly clear streets.

Alethekanon:
Transparent tracking by watchdogs prevents political slogans from substituting for actual structural housing solutions.

Awwthekanon:
Behind every data point is a human being enduring freezing nights; promises must translate into warm, safe homes.

Brothekanon:
Promises to fix homelessness sound great on day one, but until we see actual roofs over people's heads, it's a wait-and-see game.

Spirithekanon:
"If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food, and one of you says... go in peace, yet you do not give them bodily needs, what good is that?" James 2:15-16 PASS
True compassion demands tangible shelter, not mere words.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Is the government on course to end rough sleeping? – Full Fact

On his first day as Prime Minister, Andy Burnham promised to end rough sleeping.

Actual Article Body:
Everything we publish, from fact checks, investigations and in-depth analysis to comment blogs and our Government Tracker.

Browse our fact checks, explainers and analysis by topic.

Build the skills to spot bad information with practical guides, trainer-led workshops or self-paced courses you can start today.

The impact our work can make on the information environment. From proposals for changes in law and regulation to our use of AI technology and how we've been reported in the media.

Full Fact is the UK's independent fact checking charity. We put reliable evidence at the heart of public debate so you can make sense of what matters.

Pledge

“I will soon go through that door behind me and issue my first instruction: to end rough sleeping in our country.”

Andy Burnham

Our verdict

It’s too early to know how the levels of rough sleeping have changed since the pledge was made.

Rough sleeping is a form of homelessness defined by the UK government as people sleeping, or someone who is about to bed down, in “the open air” such as on the street, in parks, bus shelters, tents, doorways or other places that have not been designed for habitation such as stairwells. It doesn’t include people who are in hostels or shelters, or the hidden homeless.

Speaking outside Number 10 on the day he became Prime Minister, Andy Burnham said his first instruction would be “to end rough sleeping in our country.” In a press release issued the same day, he said: “I’m announcing this government’s commitment to finally end long-term rough sleeping across the UK at the earliest opportunity.”

Some of the language used across this announcement was unclear, particularly the exact type of rough sleeping the pledge applied to and the locations it covered.

We asked the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) if the pledge referred just to long-term rough sleeping or to both short and long-term rough sleeping, and it told us it was for both.

We also asked about the implication in the press release that the pledge refers to the entirety of the UK, despite homelessness policies being devolved and the fact each nation has its own methods of counting rough sleeping.

The MHCLG told us it will only be measuring rough sleeping in England, and acknowledged the devolved nations are responsible for their own policies. As such, we will be monitoring progress against this pledge using rough sleeping data for England.

This isn’t the first time we’ve found that the government has been unclear on the parameters of a pledge. And while we welcome the fact that more detail has since been provided, it’s important that such commitments are set out clearly to avoid confusion for voters.

Rough sleeping in England is typically measured in two main ways by the government—the rough sleeping snapshot survey, which estimates the number of people sleeping rough on a single night in autumn each year, and the rough sleeping data framework, which uses monthly information from all local authorities in England.

At the time the pledge was made, the latest rough sleeping snapshot estimated 4,793 people were sleeping rough on a single night in autumn 2025, while data framework figures estimated that in March 2026 7,541 people in England were sleeping rough.

It’s worth noting rough sleeping statistics are considered to underestimate “the true extent of rough sleeping” because they don’t account for all forms of homelessness and are thought to undercount some populations, such as women.

The government says the data framework figures are “subject to some uncertainty and should be treated as estimates” as they’re “linked to the coverage and frequency of outreach activity as well as the local data systems in place to accurately track and record this information”.

We’ve asked the MHCLG which of the two measures will be used to monitor the pledge.

No specific deadline was given for the pledge, though both the government’s initial press release and a blog published later the same week by the MHCLG referred to a broader five-year programme focused on homelessness.

We’ve also asked the MHCLG if it still stands by a previous commitment made by Sir Keir Starmer’s government to halve the number of long-term rough sleepers in England by the end of this parliament.

We’re rating this pledge as “wait and see” because while funding has been announced and the government has said it’s taking “immediate action”, it’s too early to say how estimated levels of rough sleeping have changed in England since the pledge was made.

The government said its pledge would be supported by additional funding in England, and referred to “a wider five-year programme” that will support “thousands of the people facing the most severe and long-term homelessness”.

It told us that devolved governments will receive Barnett consequentials on the homelessness and rough sleeping funding.

The MHCLG said that its initial investment will fund 1,200 homes for long-term rough sleepers and provide “intensive support” to get “at least 3,000 people” off the streets and into stable housing, as well as “immediate action” to help long-term rough sleepers move from the streets into secure accommodation.

In summer 2026 the government announced funding totalling £442 million, which it said in October would be supported by “a further £432 million” to “extend support beyond March 2027 and through to the end of this Parliament”.

A summit bringing together various groups including charities, business, health, and faith communities was held in Downing Street on 26 October 2026.

Tags

Full Fact fights for good, reliable information in the media, online, and in politics.

Andy Burnham, Prime Minister – 20 July 2026

Progress displayed publicly—so every single person in this country can judge our performance on actions, not words.

Sir Keir Starmer, then-Prime Minister – 24 September 2024

Updated  - October 28, 2026 05:30 pm IST - Jerusalem

Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, waves an Israeli flag following national election exit polls on Octobe 28, 2026
                                          | Photo Credit: Reuters

Yair Golan, leader of Israel's Democratic Party, on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) urged the Opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot to form a government in partnership with Arab-led parties to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, highlighting divisions within the opposition over such cooperation.

Several allies in the Opposition's "change bloc" have rejected the proposal to include Arab parties in a governing coalition, while some have also ruled out relying on their support from outside.

"Netanyahu lost. I know how to count to 120. 65 is more than 55. That's how Israeli democracy works. Period," Mr. Golan, a former deputy chief of staff of the Israel Defence Forces (IDF), wrote on X.

Mr. Golan called for an end to what he described as racism and fear of political cooperation with Arab citizens.

"The picture of reality must teach us one resounding lesson: We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't stop with the racism. We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he wrote.

"The voice of an Israeli citizen voting in Taybeh is worth exactly as much as the voice of an Israeli citizen voting in Givat Shmuel. No less. Not approximately. Exactly," he said, arguing that Arab citizens' votes should carry the same weight as those of Jewish citizens.

"Anyone who tries to erase the voices of Arab citizens is surrendering to Netanyahu and giving up on Israel," he added.

Mr. Golan's proposal faces resistance from Opposition figures who have ruled out forming a government that includes Arab-led parties. The Opposition remains divided over whether Arab parties should join a governing coalition or support it from outside.

Mr. Golan also challenged Mr. Netanyahu's allies over their claims to represent Zionism, criticising ultra-Orthodox parties in the Prime Minister's bloc for opposing universal military conscription.

"In Netanyahu's bloc sit 16 Knesset members from non-Zionist Haredi parties, who promote mass draft evasion while our children are fighting and dying," Mr. Golan wrote.

He argued that the opposition had a Zionist majority of its own, saying, "The Change bloc has a Zionist majority: 49 against 39. The Change bloc has an Israeli majority: 65 against 55."

Urging Opposition leaders to cooperate with Arab citizens, Mr. Golan said: "We have a majority. We have responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens. A government that will serve all Israeli citizens."

His appeal came amid uncertainty over government formation following Tuesday's (October 28) election.

According to partial results reported by Israeli media, Mr. Netanyahu's bloc had 54 seats, Eisenkot's bloc 47 and Arab-led parties 19, with 76.8% of ballot boxes counted as of 10:58 a.m. local time, according to local media reports.

A majority of 61 seats is required in the 120-member Knesset.

The figures would give Mr. Eisenkot's bloc and the Arab-led parties a combined 66 seats if the reported breakdown holds.

However, their ability to form a government would depend on whether the parties could agree on a coalition or another arrangement.

To be sure, Mr. Golan's figures of 65 and 55 in his post differ from the reported partial count and reflect his own political calculation, rather than the latest reported seat tally.

Arab-led parties have previously played a role in Israeli government formation. Ra'am, led by Mansour Abbas, joined the governing coalition formed in 2021 under then-prime minister Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. That government collapsed in 2022, triggering another election.

Mr. Bennett now leads the B'Yachad alliance, another part of the opposition whose position on cooperation with Arab parties could affect efforts to assemble a governing majority.
